figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Robust 3DGS geometry via spatially varying affine rectification. (a-c) Standard 3DGS overfits appearance, producing noisy underlying geometry. In contrast, our method extracts clean, highly accurate meshes while maintaining photorealism. (d) Monocular disparity exhibits piecewise-linear distortions, proving that a single global scale-and-shift alignment is fundamentally insufficient (scatter plot). (e) We overcome this by estimating an edge-aware spatial scale field ($\alpha_{\text{smooth}}$) to rectify the monocular depth prior, yielding geometrically consistent 3D representations.
figures.headline: Monocular disparity splits into piecewise-linear regimes, so one global scale-and-shift cannot align the whole scene.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Piecewise-linear disparity fragmentation across diverse indoor topologies. Across various scenes, the monocular depth prior consistently fractures into distinct, spatially coherent affine regimes (visualized in red, orange, and grey). The accompanying scatter plots demonstrate that fitting a single global scale-and-shift transform ($K=1$) is mathematically ill-posed, as the optimizer would be forced to average errors across fundamentally incompatible linear clusters.
figures.headline: Across scenes, monocular disparity fragments into coherent affine regions, so one global fit averages conflicting clusters.
citing_sentences: Attempting to fit a single line through the fragmented disparity space will inevitably force the optimizer to average the error across conflicting spatial clusters, resulting in the severe warping of physical geometry in some regions to satisfy the alignment of others (see Fig. 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: We compare the raw disparity predictions of (a) Metric3D-V2 and (b) MoGe against ground-truth sensor depth on the exact same scene. While the distinct network architectures allocate their local scale-and-shift parameters differently, both fundamentally exhibit the same region-dependent, piecewise-linear fragmentation. This confirms that spatial affine distortion is a systemic property of modern foundation depth models.
figures.headline: Metric3D-V2 and MoGe disparity both show the same region-dependent piecewise-linear fragmentation against sensor depth.

figures.caption: Additional qualitative comparison on NeRF-LLFF dataset. Visualized across the Flower, Fern, and Horns scenes under extreme view sparsity (rendered RGB, depth, and surface normal maps). (a) Unconstrained 3DGS severely overfits to the limited training views, resulting in massive floating artifacts and chaotic underlying geometry. (b) DRGS mitigates some artifacts via global depth alignment, but still suffers from noisy surface normals and blurred geometric details. (c) DropGaussian struggles to properly initialize in this sparse setting, leading to heavily corrupted backgrounds and incomplete structures. (d) In contrast, our proposed method leverages spatially rectified monocular priors to extract clean, highly accurate geometry with sharp object boundaries, smooth backgrounds, and highly consistent surface normals, all while preserving photorealistic appearance.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Qualitative comparisons of our proposed geometric regularization on MuSHRoom dataset. Visualized via rendered normals (top row) and depth maps (bottom row). (a) The unconstrained baseline (All off) exhibits severe geometric drift, yielding highly chaotic and noisy surface normals. (b-d) Applying individual loss terms in isolation yields incomplete geometry: while $\mathcal{L}_{\text{depth}}$ anchors global scale, it fails to resolve high-frequency structural noise, and while $\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}}$ or $\mathcal{L}_{\text{normal}}$ improve local structure, they struggle without an absolute metric anchor. (h) Our full formulation combines these constraints. By anchoring the global metric scale while explicitly enforcing local spatial gradients and physical orientations, the complete approach reconstructs exceptionally clean planar surfaces (e.g.,, the walls and ceiling), sharp structural boundaries, and globally consistent depth.

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its underlying geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically relying on a global linear alignment. Crucially, we reveal a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This phenomenon invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which inevitably warp scene geometry by enforcing a single scale-and-shift transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that dynamically corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our sensor-free approach prevents structural collapse under extreme view sparsity and extracts highly accurate 3D meshes, effectively bridging the gap toward sensor-supervised geometric fidelity while preserving state-of-the-art photorealism.

sections.body: The paper argues that 3DGS geometry lags its rendering quality and that monocular depth priors are usually fit with one global scale-and-shift transform. It reports that Depth-Anything-V2, MoGe and Metric3D-V2 produce region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions, with breaks along object boundaries and large depth discontinuities. The authors propose spatially varying affine fields, estimated from disparity and rendered depth gradients, that need no sensor depth. The listed contributions are the distortion finding, the affine rectification model, and a gradient-domain regularizer that couples disparity gradients with 3DGS depth and normals. Quantitative evidence is deferred to the experiments.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Monocular depth priors show region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions, so global alignment breaks down for 3DGS geometry.

sections.body: Related work covers Structure-from-Motion, Multi-View Stereo, NeRF and explicit representations including 3DGS. It describes 3DGS pipelines that add monocular depth and jointly optimize a single global scale-and-shift transform, which the paper says fails under the distortions shown in Section 3.1. Other 3DGS extensions change the primitives, for example into 2D patches or disks, with appended normals, or through signed-distance fields. The paper states its method keeps the Gaussian representation unchanged and corrects spatially varying distortions in the monocular prior instead of enforcing rigid global alignment.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior depth-guided 3DGS methods fit one global scale-and-shift, and other extensions alter Gaussian primitives instead.

sections.body: The method fits spatially varying fields $\alpha$ and $\beta$ so that inverse disparity matches rendered depth, using $\frac{1}{d(u,v)}=\alpha(u,v)\mathcal{D}(u,v)+\beta(u,v)$ as the model. Scale is estimated from the ratio of finite-difference gradient magnitudes, shift is recovered from the affine relation, and both fields are smoothed with a guided filter that uses disparity as the guide. Table 1 reports inlier ratios of 58.9% for one global transform and 92.7% for five local regions on MuSHRoom at a 0.02 threshold. A normal-aware gradient loss and an L1 depth loss, after a global least-squares re-alignment, complete the regularization. The fields are re-estimated at every iteration.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Spatially varying scale and shift fields rectify monocular disparity, then drive normal-aware gradient and depth losses.

sections.body: Experiments train 3DGS for 30k iterations with Depth-Anything-V2-Large priors and leave the densification logic unchanged. Sparse-view tests on NeRF-LLFF use 2 to 5 training views, averaged over ten random seeds, and compare against DRGS, DropGaussian and DepthSplat. On MuSHRoom, the method's Abs Rel is 0.0551 / 0.0490, while the monocular-prior DN-Splatter (Monodepth) baseline reaches 0.3542 / 0.3669. Mesh results on MuSHRoom and ScanNet++ use TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction depending on the method. The paper notes that loss weights were reduced on the kokko and sauna scenes because the default weights produced floaters.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: The method cuts MuSHRoom Abs Rel to 0.0551 / 0.0490, versus 0.3542 / 0.3669 for DN-Splatter (Monodepth).

sections.body: The conclusion restates the problem: global linear alignment fails under region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions in monocular depth. It summarizes the spatially varying affine rectification and the normal-aware gradient coupling, and says these require no architectural change to 3DGS. The paper states the approach significantly outperforms sensor-free depth-regularized baselines across NeRF-LLFF, MuSHRoom and ScanNet++, and outperforms explicit baselines on NeRF-LLFF and MuSHRoom. It concludes the method bridges the gap toward sensor-supervised geometric fidelity. This section gives no new numbers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The method approaches sensor-supervised geometric fidelity without any physical depth input.

sections.body: The appendix expands the distortion analysis in Tables 7 to 10, covering Metric3D-V2, MoGe and Depth-Anything-V2 on MuSHRoom and Depth-Anything-V2 on ScanNet++ at residual thresholds of 0.005, 0.02 and 0.05. It reports that Depth-Anything-V2 with one global transform aligns 25.6% of MuSHRoom geometry at the strict threshold. Additional figures cover distortions, sparse-view NeRF-LLFF comparisons, MuSHRoom and ScanNet++ qualitative results, and loss ablations. The limitations section covers dependence on the monocular model, the lack of absolute physical scale, and sensitivity to regularization strength. It notes an F-score of 0.18 on scene b20a261fdf, compared with 0.46 on 8b5caf3398.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists distortion tables across models and thresholds, extra figures, per-scene results and limitations.
